benchmark_details.name: MuSR
benchmark_details.overview: MuSR is a benchmark that measures free text narrative reasoning corresponding to real-world domains of reasoning. It is more challenging than other synthetically-crafted benchmarks while remaining tractable for human annotators.

purpose_and_intended_users.goal: To evaluate LLMs and prompting techniques on robust reasoning using free text narratives.

data.source: The data is generated as free text narratives; the construction process involves diversity sampling, chaptering, and tree validators.
data.annotation: For human evaluation, 7 annotators were used (4 authors and 3 hired undergraduate students). Instances were triply-annotated (34 instances for Murder Mystery and Team Allocation, 40 for Object Placements). The annotation quality is assessed via lowest, highest, average, and majority vote scores. The majority vote score is considered reflective of the ceiling for human performance.

methods: Models are evaluated using prompting techniques, including chain-of-thought.
A variant of Program-Aided Language Models (PAL) is run on the Team Allocation domain.
methodology.interpretation: Higher scores indicate better performance (since MUSR is a continuous metric where lower_is_better is false).
methodology.baseline_results: Based on 1 model evaluations from Every Eval Ever: mean MUSR = 0.4413 (std = 0.0000). Top performers: YiSM-blossom5.1-34B-SLERP (0.4413).
methodology.validation: Human evaluation with multiple annotators was conducted to validate that answers derived from the formal representation match what can be derived from the narratives.

description: Unrepresentative data occurs when the training or fine-tuning data is not sufficiently representative of the underlying population or does not measure the phenomenon of interest. Synthetic data might not fully capture the complexity and nuances of real-world data. Causes include possible limitations in the seed data quality, biases in generation methods, or inadequate domain knowledge. Thus, AI models might struggle to generalize effectively to real-world scenarios.
possible_risks.concern: If the data is not representative, then the model will not work as intended.

description: AI model risks are socio-technical, so their testing needs input from a broad set of disciplines and diverse testing practices.
possible_risks.concern: Without diversity and the relevant experience, an organization might not correctly or completely identify and test for AI risks.

description: Historical and societal biases might be present in data that are used to train and fine-tune models. Biases can also be inherited from seed data or exacerbated by synthetic data generation methods.
possible_risks.concern: Training an AI system on data with bias, such as historical or societal bias, can lead to biased or skewed outputs that can unfairly represent or otherwise discriminate against certain groups or individuals.

description: Data contamination occurs when incorrect data is used for training. For example, data that is not aligned with model’s purpose or data that is already set aside for other development tasks such as testing and evaluation.
possible_risks.concern: Data that differs from the intended training data might skew model accuracy and affect model outcomes.

description: Generated content might unfairly represent certain groups or individuals.
possible_risks.concern: Bias can harm users of the AI models and magnify existing discriminatory behaviors.
